column2: Endowed with virtue and goodness, freed from darkness and from weariness, all of them, possessed of every excellence, went each to his own place.
Whatever each one desired, at that time, Vyasa, the giver of boons, devoted to dharma, sent each away accordingly.
Hearing of the kings' return, the people rejoiced, glad, even those who had gone into other bodies.
The man who hears of this meeting of those with their dear ones always gains what is dear, both here and after death.
The wise man who recites this obtains union with beloved kin, without effort and without sickness, and reaches the highest perfection.
Men devoted to study and to ritual action, O Bharata, steadfast people devoted to the discipline of the self, who always hear this parva, will attain the highest goal.
Joyful, he asked about the return: "How, indeed, is there a seeing again of the form of those who have cast off their bodies?"
Thus addressed, that glorious best of brahmins, Vyasa's disciple, best of speakers, replied to King Janamejaya.

It is certain that no action is ever lost; bodies are born of action, and so are their forms, O king.
mahabharata:15:42.5	The great elements are eternal, resting on the Lord of beings; they dwell together always, and in separation there is no destruction.
mahabharata:15:42.6	An action done is not for destruction; its fruit surely comes. The self, joined with these, experiences pleasure and pain.
mahabharata:15:42.7	The knower of the field is imperishable and eternal, so it is settled; that state of being the self of creatures is fixed, for those who understand.
mahabharata:15:42.8	As long as action is not exhausted, so long does one keep one's own form; when action is exhausted, a man takes on a different form.
mahabharata:15:42.9	Joined together, taking a body, the many natures become one; and so they are eternal, for those who know separateness.
mahabharata:15:42.11	I tell you this, O king, if it is dear to you: you have heard the paths of the gods in the arrangement of the sacrifice.
Where your sacrifice was well done, there the gods were favourable to you; when the gods are assembled, the lords of the movement of beasts, going with that sacrifice, others are not eternal.
In this eternal group of five and in the eternal self, the man who sees their various joining in vain, grieves greatly at separation; he is a child, I think.
He who sees fault in separation should renounce union here; where there is no attachment there is no meeting, and the sorrow on earth born of separation.
One who knows the higher and the lower is not roused by pride; the one who does not know, touching the highest understanding, is freed from delusion.
Fallen from the unseen, and gone again to the unseen: I do not know him, he does not know me, and I have no lack of dispassion.
By whatever body this helpless one acts, by that very body he must experience it; he obtains the mental by the mind, and the bodily, being embodied, by the body."
That king, best of men, obtained the duties of kings and the Brahmic Upanishad, and also firmness of understanding.
And the greatly wise Vidura attained perfection through the power of austerity; Dhritarashtra, having gone to Vyasa, the ascetic, also.
Janamejaya said: "If Vyasa, giver of boons, would show me my father in that form, dress and age, I would believe all of it.
It would be dear to me, and I would be fulfilled and resolved; by the grace of the sage's son, let my desire be accomplished."
Sauti said: When the king had spoken, the mighty and wise Vyasa showed favour and brought Parikshit.
Then King Janamejaya saw his father, the glorious king, come from heaven in that same form and age.
He saw also the great-souled Shamika and his son Shringin, and the ministers of the king who had been there.
Then, at the closing bath, King Janamejaya, delighted, bathed his father, and the king bathed himself.
Astika said: "This sacrifice is of many wonders, I think, since today my father has come, destroyer of my grief.
Astika said: By the sage Dvaipayana, the ancient treasure of austerity, O best of the Kuru line, both worlds were won through your sacrifice.
O delight of the Pandavas, you have heard a wondrous tale; the serpents were reduced to ashes and went to your father's path.
Somehow Takshaka was released, because of your truthfulness, O king; all the sages were honoured, having seen the great soul's fate.
Very great dharma has been obtained by hearing what destroys sin; the knot of the heart is loosed by the sight of noble people.
Those who side with dharma and delight in good conduct, whose sight removes sin, to them reverent bows should be made."
Sauti said: Hearing this from the best of brahmins, King Janamejaya honoured that sage, again and again showing him respect.
And he asked the sage Vaishampayana, the unfailing one, knowing dharma, best among the good, for the particulars of the tale of the forest dwelling.
Vaishampayana said: Having seen that great marvel, the seeing of his sons again, the royal sage, free from grief, went back to the hermitage.
All the other people and the great sages returned as they wished, with Dhritarashtra's leave.
But the great-souled Pandavas, their soldiers mostly reduced, followed the great king with his wife.
When he had gone to the hermitage, the wise brahmin sage honoured by the worlds, the son of Satyavati, said to Dhritarashtra:

Dhritarashtra, mighty-armed joy of the Kurus, listen: you have heard the various talks of sages old in knowledge and holy in deed,
mahabharata:15:44.7	of those elders of high lineage, who know the Vedas and their limbs, knowers of dharma, ancient, as they speak.
mahabharata:15:44.8	Do not set your mind on grief; the wise man is not pained over what he longs for. You have heard the secret of the gods from Narada, who has seen the gods.
mahabharata:15:44.9	Your sons have gone by the dharma of kshatriyas to the auspicious goal purified by weapons, as you saw them, moving about at will.
mahabharata:15:44.10	This wise Yudhishthira waits upon you, with all his brothers, his wife and his friends.
mahabharata:15:44.11	Send him away; let him go to rule his own kingdom. More than a month has already passed for them living in the forest.
mahabharata:15:44.12	This seat must always be guarded with effort, O scorcher of foes; for this thing called a kingdom has many rivals, O lord of men.
Thus addressed by Vyasa of boundless wisdom, the Kuru king, eloquent, called Yudhishthira and spoke these words.

Ajatashatru, blessings on you; hear me with your brothers. By your grace, O lord of the earth, grief does not trouble us.
mahabharata:15:44.15	I was happy with you as with sons in Gajasahvaya; a wise man, led by a protector who treated those dear to him kindly.
mahabharata:15:44.16	I have received from you the fruit of having sons; my joy in you is great; I feel no anger, mighty-armed one; go, son, without delay.
mahabharata:15:44.17	Seeing you here, my austerity is diminished; and this body, joined to austerity, was kept alive again on seeing you.
mahabharata:15:44.18	These two mothers of yours, eating fallen leaves, keeping vows like mine, son, will not live long.
mahabharata:15:44.19	Duryodhana and the others have been seen gone to the other worlds, through the power of Vyasa's austerity and by meeting you.
mahabharata:15:44.20	The purpose of my life, sinless one, has long been fulfilled; I will take up fierce austerity; you ought to permit it.
mahabharata:15:44.21	In you today the funeral cake, the fame and this family are established; today or tomorrow, mighty-armed one, go, son, without delay.
mahabharata:15:44.22	You have heard much of statecraft, best of the Bharatas; I see nothing more to instruct you in, lord; so much is done.
When he had spoken, the king, dear one, said to the king: "You should not abandon me, knower of dharma, who am without fault.
Let all my brothers and followers go as they please; I will wait on you and the two mothers of restrained vows."
Then Gandhari said to him: "Not so, son; listen to me. The Kuru line depends on you, and the funeral offering of my father-in-law.
Go, son; this much is enough; we have been honoured. What the king says must be done by you, son, for it is your father's word."
Thus told by Gandhari, he spoke these words to Kunti, wiping his eyes, filled with tears of love, as she wept.

The king sends me away, and so does the renowned Gandhari; but with my mind bound to you, how shall I go, in sorrow?
mahabharata:15:44.29	I cannot bear to cause an obstacle to your austerity, practiser of dharma; for there is nothing higher than austerity, and by austerity one attains greatness.
mahabharata:15:44.30	Nor, O queen, is my mind set on the kingdom as it once was; my mind is wholly devoted to austerity.
mahabharata:15:44.31	This whole earth is empty and gives me no joy, fair lady; our kinsmen are destroyed, and our strength is not as it was before.
mahabharata:15:44.32	The Panchalas are greatly diminished, only girls and mothers left; I see no one, auspicious one, who can carry on their line.
mahabharata:15:44.33	All were reduced to ashes by Drona alone in battle, and the rest were slain at night by Drona's son.
mahabharata:15:44.34	We saw the Chedis and the Matsyas before as well; only the circle of the Vrishnis remains, under the protection of Vasudeva, whom I wish to see only for the sake of dharma and wealth, for no other reason.
mahabharata:15:44.35	Look on us all with kindness; to see you will be hard, mother, for the king will begin fierce austerity.
Hearing this, mighty-armed Sahadeva, lord of warriors, his eyes dimmed with tears, said this to Yudhishthira:

I cannot bear to abandon my mother, best of kings; you may go back quickly; I shall practise austerity in the forest.
mahabharata:15:44.38	Here I will dry up my body with austerity, devoted to serving the feet of the king and of these two mothers.
Then Kunti embraced the mighty-armed one and said to him: "Go, son; do not speak so, but do as I say.
May your journeys be auspicious, may you be well, my sons; there would be an obstruction to our austerity in this.
Bound by the cord of love for you, I would fall from austerity; therefore go, my son; little time remains to us, lord."
Thus with Kunti's many words Sahadeva's mind was steadied, O king of kings, and the king's especially.
Permitted by their mother and the king, the bulls of the Kuru line bowed to the best of the Kurus and began to take their leave.
O king, we shall return, welcomed with blessings; with your leave, O king, we shall go, free from fault.
Thus addressed by the great-souled king of dharma, the royal sage gave his leave, rejoicing in Yudhishthira with blessings of victory.
The king comforted Bhima, best of the strong, and he, wise and valiant, rightly received it.
Embracing Arjuna and the two twins, bulls among men, that Kuru descendant gave his leave, embracing and rejoicing over them.
Permitted also by Gandhari, they bowed at her feet, were smelled on the head and embraced by their mother, and circled the king, like calves when held back.
Looking back again and again, they went off after circling him, and so did virtuous Draupadi and all the Kuru women.
Having rightly offered their service to the father-in-law, they departed, permitted by the two mothers-in-law, embraced and blessed, instructed in what was to be done, and went with their husbands.
Then arose the cry of the charioteers, "Yoke up!", the bellowing of camels and the neighing of horses.
Then King Yudhishthira, with his wife and soldiers and kinsmen, returned again to the city of Hastinapura.
Having honoured him, mighty-armed Yudhishthira, king of the Kurus, best of speakers, said to him as he sat at ease:

After a long time I see the venerable one arrived. Is it well with you, brahmin, or has some good come to you?
mahabharata:15:45.4	Which lands have you seen, and what can I do for you? Tell me, chief of brahmins; you are our dear guest.
Narada said: "I am long seen by you, O king; I have come from the forest of austerity; I have seen holy places, and the Ganga too, O king."
Yudhishthira said: "People dwelling on the Ganga's bank tell me that the great-souled Dhritarashtra has taken up supreme austerity.
Did you see him there, that bull of the Kurus, in health, and Gandhari and Pritha, and Sanjaya the charioteer's son?
And how does my father, that king, fare today? I wish to hear, venerable one, if you have seen the king."
Narada said: "Be steady, great king, and hear all just as it was, as I heard and saw it in that forest of austerity.
With Gandhari, the wise one, and with the daughter-in-law Kunti, and with Sanjaya the charioteer, with the sacred fires and priests,
your father, rich in austerity, took up fierce austerity; holding a pebble in his mouth, the sage lived on air.
Honoured by all the sages in the forest, that great ascetic became only skin and bone for six months.
Gandhari lived on water, Kunti fasted for a month at a time, and Sanjaya lived on one meal in six, O Bharata.
And the priests there offered into the fires duly, lord, the king being sometimes seen and sometimes unseen in that forest.
The king became homeless and a wanderer of the forest; and the two queens and Sanjaya followed him together.
Sanjaya was the king's guide on level and uneven ground, and blameless Pritha, O king, was Gandhari's eye.
Then once, on the Ganga's bank, that best of kings, the wise one, bathed in the Ganga and turned toward the hermitage.
Then a wind arose and a great forest fire began; it burned that whole forest, enclosing it on every side.
As herds of deer burned all around, and snakes, and herds of boars crowded to the waters,
in that forest thrown into turmoil, in this supreme calamity, the king, weak in breath and movement from fasting, was unable to flee, and your two mothers were very thin.
Then the king, seeing the fire coming near, said to the charioteer Sanjaya, O lord of the earth:
'Go, Sanjaya, where fire will never burn you; we, joined with this fire, shall go to the highest goal.'
Troubled, Sanjaya, best of speakers, said to him: 'O king, this death by fire will be unwelcome and in vain for you.
I see no means of saving you from the fire; whatever is to be done next, you ought to tell me.'
Thus told by Sanjaya, the king said again: 'This is not an unwelcome death for us, who have left our house of our own accord.
Water, fire, wind, or even starvation are praised for ascetics; go, Sanjaya, without delay.'
Having said this to Sanjaya, the king collected his mind and sat facing east with Gandhari and Kunti.
Seeing him so, Sanjaya circled him and said to him, "Join your self, lord."
The wise sage's son, the king, did as he said; restraining the host of the senses, he sat then like a log of wood.
The greatly fortunate Gandhari and your mother Pritha, and the king your father, were joined with the forest fire.
But Sanjaya, the great minister, escaped from that fire; I saw him on the Ganga's bank, surrounded by ascetics.
The radiant Sanjaya, having taken leave of them and reported all this fully, departed to the mountain Himavat.
Thus did the great-minded king of the Kurus meet his end, and Gandhari and Pritha, your two mothers, O lord of men.
Following by chance, I saw the king's body and the bodies of both queens, O best of the Bharatas.
Then in that forest of austerity the ascetics assembled; hearing of the king's end, they did not grieve for his fate.
There I heard all this, best of men, how the king was burned and your two mothers, O Pandava.
You should not grieve, king of kings; that lord of the earth is well, having gone through union with fire, and so are Gandhari and your mother."
Vaishampayana said: Hearing this, a great grief arose in all the great-souled Pandavas at Dhritarashtra's passing.
A great cry of anguish rose from the women of the inner apartments, and from the townspeople, O great king, hearing of the king's end.
Alas, shame! cried the king, deeply grieved, and with arms upraised Yudhishthira wept, remembering his mother, and all his brothers with Bhimasena at their head.
And in the inner apartments a very great sound of weeping arose, O great king, on hearing that Pritha had gone so.
They all grieved for the old king, burned, who had lost his sons, and for the ascetic Gandhari.
When that noise had subsided, after a short while, O Bharata, holding back his tears with fortitude, Dharmaraja spoke thus.

The destinies of men are hard to understand, I think, when the son of Vichitravirya was burned thus by a forest fire.
mahabharata:15:46.3	He who had a hundred splendid sons, the strong-armed king with the strength of ten thousand elephants, was burned by a forest fire.
mahabharata:15:46.4	He whom fine women once fanned with palm-leaf fans, vultures fanned, driven by the forest fire.
mahabharata:15:46.5	He who lay and was awakened by throngs of bards and heralds now lies on the ground, king, through the deeds of my sin.
mahabharata:15:46.6	But I do not grieve for Gandhari, renowned, her sons slain, who has gone to her husband's world, standing firm in the vow of a wife.
mahabharata:15:46.7	I grieve only for Pritha, who gave up the great blazing prosperity of her sons' kingdom and chose the forest life.
mahabharata:15:46.8	Shame on this kingdom of ours, shame on strength, shame on valour, and on the dharma of kshatriyas, since we live though dead.
mahabharata:15:46.9	Very subtle indeed is the course of Time, best of brahmins, that she gave up the kingdom and chose to live in the forest.
mahabharata:15:46.10	The mother of Yudhishthira, of Bhima and of Vijaya, burned like one without a protector; I am bewildered thinking of it.
mahabharata:15:46.11	In vain was Agni satisfied by Savyasachin at Khandava, not knowing the favour done; he was ungrateful, I think.
mahabharata:15:46.12	That blessed one who burned the mother of Savyasachin, he who once came disguised as a brahmin begging alms; shame on Agni, and shame on Partha's famed truthfulness.
mahabharata:15:46.13	And this seems to me still more painful, venerable one, that the lord of the earth met a fire in vain.
mahabharata:15:46.14	And how could such a death befall that ascetic royal sage of the Kurus, after he had ruled this earth?
mahabharata:15:46.15	While his fires, purified with mantras, stood in the great forest, my father came to his end joined with a fire in vain.
I think Pritha, trembling, thin, her veins showing, cried out in great terror, "Ah, dear Dharmaraja!"
Bhima, save me from this fear! she cried, and my mother was surrounded on every side by the forest fire.
Sahadeva was dearer to her than her own sons, yet the hero, son of Madri, did not rescue her.
Hearing that, they all wept, embracing one another, the five Pandavas, tormented with grief, like beings at the end of an age.
The sound of those weeping lords of men, shut in by the vast palace, filled heaven and earth.

We have heard that when that wise one, living on air, entered the forest, the fires were abandoned after he had made a sacrifice.
mahabharata:15:47.3	The priests then left those fires in the lonely forest and went where they wished, best of the Bharatas.
mahabharata:15:47.4	It is said that fire grew great in that forest then; the ascetics told me that by it the forest was set ablaze.
mahabharata:15:47.5	That king, on the Jahnavi's bank, as I have told you, was joined with his own fire, best of the Bharatas.
mahabharata:15:47.6	So the sages told me, sinless one, those whom I saw on the bank of the Bhagirathi, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:15:47.7	Thus the king was joined with his own fire, lord of the earth; do not grieve, for he has gone to the highest goal.
mahabharata:15:47.8	Your mother, Pandava, by serving her elders has attained great perfection; I have no doubt of it.
mahabharata:15:47.9	You ought to perform the water-offering for them, descendant of Kuru; let this be done here by you with all your brothers.
The townspeople and country folk, led by devotion to the king, went to the Ganga on all sides, each wrapped in a single cloth.
Then all those bulls of the Kurus, entering the water, with Yuyutsu in front, gave water to the great-souled ones.
They made the water-offerings for Gandhari and for Pritha rightly, by name and lineage, and finished the purification, staying there outside the city.
The best of the Kurus sent men who knew the rites and were trustworthy to Gangadvara, where the king had been burned.
There at Gangadvara the king commanded the men to perform the due rites for them, giving what had to be given.
On the twelfth day, his purification done, the Pandava king duly gave the funeral offerings with fees.
In Dhritarashtra's name the lord of the earth gave gold, silver, cows and costly beds.
And the radiant king gave unsurpassed gifts separately for Gandhari and for Pritha, declaring their names.
Whatever each brahmin wished, and as much as he wished, he received: a bed, food, a vehicle, jewels and wealth.
The king gave vehicles, clothing, comforts, and maidservants as attendants, in the name of those two mothers.
Then the lord of the earth, the wise one, having given funeral offerings many times, entered again the city called Varanavata's rival, Hastinapura.
And the men who had gone at the king's word, having arranged the rites for them, came back again.
Having honoured them duly with garlands and various perfumes, they arranged their rites and reported to the king.
Having comforted the righteous King Yudhishthira, Narada, the great sage, went away as he wished, O king.
Thus passed three years of the wise Dhritarashtra in the forest, after ten and five in the city.
He had lost his sons in the war, and always gave gifts to kinsmen, relatives, friends, brothers and his own people.
But King Yudhishthira, not very glad at heart then, bore that kingdom, his kinsmen and relatives slain.
Seated there, all the subjects, the brahmins and the townsmen surrounded him and stood around.
To all those dejected, still, bereft of sense, Partha, himself still more dejected, spoke these words.
Thus addressed by Partha of untiring deeds, the citizens quickly made ready, eager for their own welfare.
That night Partha stayed in Keshava's house, suddenly overwhelmed by great grief and bewilderment.
At daybreak mighty Vasudeva, the son of Shura, of great splendour, having yoked himself in yoga, went to the highest goal.
Then a great and terrible sound arose in Vasudeva's house from the women crying out and weeping.
All the women, their hair dishevelled, their ornaments and garlands cast off, beating their breasts with their hands, lamented piteously.
Devaki, Bhadra, Rohini and Madira, the best of women, resolved to follow their husband.
Then Partha had Shauri carried out of the city on a great bier borne by men, with many garlands, O Bharata.
The townspeople of Dvaraka, all of them, O bull among men, followed him there, wrapped in grief and sorrow.
His horse-sacrifice umbrella and the blazing fires went before his bier, and the priests went with them.
The goddess-like queens, richly adorned, followed that hero, surrounded by thousands of women and thousands of daughters-in-law.
At the place that had been dear to him while he lived, the great soul, they laid him down and performed the funeral rites for the dead.
When that hero, the son of Shura, lay on the pyre, his four wives, the best of women, mounted it and went to their husband's world.
The son of Pandu had him burned with the four women, with sandalwood and various perfumes, high and low.
Then arose the sound of the kindled fire, the chanting of the Sama singers, and the weeping of men.
Then the young Vrishni heroes, with Vajra at their head, and the women, all offered water for the great soul.
Having had that rite performed, Phalguna, who never abandoned dharma, went to where the Vrishnis had been destroyed, O bull of the Bharatas.
Seeing them fallen in the slaughter, he was deeply grieved, that descendant of Kuru, and did what the time required.
Those killed by the Brahmin's curse, with clubs born of the eraka reed, he performed all rites for, chiefly as was fitting.
Then, searching for the bodies of Rama and Vasudeva both, he had them burned by trustworthy men.
Having duly performed their funeral rites, on the seventh day the Pandava set out hastily, mounting a chariot, with chariots yoked to horses and also with those drawn by cows, asses and camels.
The wives of the Vrishni heroes, weeping, wasted with grief, followed the great-souled son of Pandu, Dhananjaya.
The servants of the Andhakas and Vrishnis, the charioteers, and the townsfolk and country people, with the heroless, the old and the children, went, surrounding the women, at Partha's command.
Elephant-riders went on elephants like mountains, and men with foot-guards and with weapons ready went along.
The sons of the Andhakas and Vrishnis, devoted to Partha, with brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and wealthy shudras,
sixteen thousand women of Vasudeva's household went with Vajra, the grandson of wise Krishna, in front.
Many thousands, tens of thousands and hundreds of millions of women of the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, their protectors slain, went out.
That great and wealthy host of the Vrishnis, like the sea, was led by Partha, best of charioteers, the conqueror of hostile cities.
When those people had gone out, the sea, home of sea-monsters, flooded Dvaraka, full of jewels, with water.
Seeing that marvel, the people of Dvaraka went faster and faster, saying, "Ah, fate!"
Dwelling in lovely forests, on mountains and by rivers, Dhananjaya led the Vrishni women on.
The wise lord reached the Panchanada country, very prosperous, rich in cattle and grain, and made his halt there.
Then greed arose in the robbers, their rulers slain, seeing the women being led by Partha alone, O Bharata.
Then those sinful Abhiras, their minds ruined by greed, of ill aspect, assembled and took counsel.
This one Arjuna is the only warrior; he leads us past, taking the old, the children and the lordless, and these warriors have lost their vigour.
Then those robbers armed with staves, by the thousand, plunderers, ran at the Vrishnis' people.
Frightening the common folk with a great lion's roar, they attacked for the sake of wealth, driven by the turn of time.
Then the son of Kunti turned back suddenly with his followers, and mighty-armed Arjuna, smiling as it were, said to them:
Turn back, you who do not know dharma, if you do not wish to die; you will grieve when you are slain by me, pierced by arrows.
Though so told by the hero, scorning his words, the fools attacked the people, though held back again and again.
Then Arjuna began to string the divine, great, ageless bow Gandiva, as if only with effort.
He strung it with difficulty amid the confused tumult; he thought of his weapons, but he did not remember them.
Seeing that great failure in the strength of his arms in battle, and the loss of his divine great weapons, he was ashamed.
And all those Vrishni warriors, riding elephants, horses and chariots, could not turn back the people being carried off.
But because the women were so many, falling here and there, Partha made an effort to protect the people.
While all the warriors looked on, those excellent women were dragged away on every side, and others went off of their own will.
Then Partha Dhananjaya, troubled, killed robbers with arrows loosed from Gandiva, with the Vrishni servants, lord.
In a moment, O king, his straight-flying arrows were exhausted; once inexhaustible, they were spent, feeding on blood.
Reaching the end of his arrows, struck with grief and sorrow, the son of Indra then killed robbers with the tip of his bow.
While Partha looked on, those barbarians, taking the best women of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, went off in every direction, O Janamejaya.
But Dhananjaya, the lord, thought of that as fate, overcome with grief and sorrow, sighing deeply.
With the loss of his weapons, the failing of his arm's strength, the bow's disobedience and the exhaustion of his arrows,
Partha became despondent, thinking, "It is fate," and turned back, O king, saying, "This is not so."
Then that greatly wise one, taking what remained of the women, whose best jewels had been carried off, came down to Kurukshetra.
Thus bringing the remnant of the Vrishni women, Dhananjaya, the Kuru descendant, settled them here and there.
The best of men settled the son of Hridika in the city of Martikavata, and the remaining women of the Bhoja king.
Then the Pandava, taking the old, the children and the women, all bereft of heroes, settled them in Indraprastha.
The righteous one settled Yuyudhana's son, Satyaki's dear child, on the Sarasvati, with the old and the children placed before him.
At Indraprastha he gave the kingdom to Vajra, slayer of heroes; but Akrura's wives, though they were held back, went off to the forest.
Rukmini, Gandhari, Shaibya, Haimavati and the goddess Jambavati entered the fire.
Satyabhama and other beloved wives of Krishna, O king, entered the forest, resolved on austerity.
The men of Dvaraka who followed Partha, he divided as was fitting and gave over to Vajra.
Having done what the time required, Arjuna, his face covered with tears, saw Krishna Dvaipayana, O king, seated in his hermitage.
Approaching that knower of dharma, of great vows, he waited on him, announced his name to him, "I am Arjuna," and bowed.
Welcome to you, said the sage, the son of Satyavati; and the great sage, with a gracious mind, said, "Be seated."
